title: Yukgaejang
subtitle: Spicy shredded beef and vegetable soup
excerpt: A deeply red, fiery Korean soup made by simmering a whole piece of beef until tender, then shredding it and returning it to a broth built with gochugaru, garlic, and spring onions. It serves 4 and takes about 80 minutes. It is one of the most fortifying soups in Korean cooking.
sourceNotes: Yukgaejang has roots in the royal court dish gaejangguk, which dates back to the Joseon dynasty. The modern version developed as a warming, restorative soup eaten during summer heat to replenish energy, following the Korean tradition of iyeol chiyeol, fighting heat with heat. It remains one of the dishes most closely associated with Korean summer eating.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in portions for up to 2 months. Defrost in the fridge overnight and reheat gently, adding a splash of water if needed.

glossaryTerms.definition: Gochugaru is Korean red chilli powder made from sun-dried red peppers. It ranges from mild to hot and has a slightly smoky, fruity quality distinct from generic chilli flakes. It is used in enormous quantities in Korean cooking, colouring soups and stews a vivid red and providing warmth without the sharp bite of some other chillies.

The name yukgaejang breaks down as yuk (meat, specifically beef), gae (a reference to the spiced gaejangguk soup from which it descends), and jang (sauce or seasoning). The dish is essentially a beef-based descendant of an older spiced broth tradition from the Joseon court era. It is one of the classic tang (soup) dishes of Korean cooking.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes about 80 minutes in total.
is a deeply spiced Korean beef soup in which a whole piece of sirloin is simmered until tender, shredded into strips, and returned to a broth coloured and heated with
. Bean sprouts, spinach, and spring onions are added near the end to keep them vibrant.

The key technique here is blooming the gochugaru in sesame oil before adding it to the broth. Heating the chilli powder briefly in oil extracts its colour and flavour far more effectively than adding it directly to water. Do this in a separate pan, then stir the chilli oil into the simmering broth. The soup should be a vivid, deep red.

content.text: Place the whole piece of beef in a large pot with 1.5 litres of cold water. Bring to the boil, skimming off any grey foam that rises. Reduce the heat, cover, and simmer for 40 minutes until the beef is tender and pulls apart with a fork.
Lift the beef out and set aside to cool slightly. Reserve the broth in the pot.
Shred the beef by hand into long strips, following the grain. Set aside.
In a small pan or ladle set over medium heat, warm the sesame oil. Add the gochugaru and garlic and stir for 1 minute until fragrant and the oil is deeply red. Do not let it burn.
Add the chilli oil mixture to the beef broth and stir well. Bring back to a simmer.
Add the shredded beef, soy sauce, and fish sauce. Simmer for 5 minutes.

Add the bean sprouts, spring onions, and spinach. Cook for a further 5 minutes until all vegetables are tender. Taste and adjust seasoning with soy sauce or fish sauce. Serve in deep bowls with steamed rice.

items.symptom: The broth is not red enough
items.cause: The gochugaru was not bloomed properly in the oil or too little was used
items.fix: Add gochugaru a spoonful at a time and taste as you go. The heat builds with cooking time. Start mild and increase at the end.

items.symptom: The beef is tough and does not shred easily
items.cause: The sirloin needs longer simmering to break down the fibres
items.fix: Return the beef to the broth and simmer covered for another 15 to 20 minutes before attempting to shred again

items.cause: Gochugaru brands vary widely in heat level
items.fix: Add more broth or water to dilute, and season back up with soy sauce and a pinch of salt

content.text: Yukgaejang is one of the dishes most closely linked to the Korean concept of iyeol chiyeol, the idea that eating hot, spicy food in summer helps the body cool down by triggering sweat. It is a summer soup in Korea, commonly eaten during the hottest days of the year. In practice, it is also eaten year-round as a restorative meal. The combination of beef, chilli, and vegetables makes it filling and nourishing. It is served in deep bowls over rice and eaten slowly.
